slides.title: Affine Quadrics
slides.notes: Open by framing affine quadrics as the first nonlinear class where the algebra still feels like linear algebra. The audience should see that the single equation is not merely a shape recipe. It contains a symmetric bilinear form, a translation problem, a topology problem, and later a Euclidean measurement problem once rotations and lengths are allowed.

slides.title: Reduction Workflow
slides.notes: Use this slide as the organizing promise for the lecture. The key distinction is between a remembered catalog and a reproducible reduction. Students should leave with an algorithmic habit: symmetrize, translate when possible, diagonalize, inspect the nullspace, and only then attach the familiar names ellipsoid, hyperboloid, cone, paraboloid, or cylinder.

slides.title: Translation Identity
slides.notes: The translation formula is the main algebraic engine of the chapter. Work through it slowly enough that the center condition appears naturally rather than as a definition dropped from the sky. The surviving term is the diagnostic: if the coefficient of y vanishes, the quadric is centered; if it cannot vanish in a null direction, parabolic geometry remains.

slides.title: Center Or Parabolic Direction
slides.notes: Let the figure do real work here. The point is that completing squares is not just a symbolic trick; it tells us whether the origin can be moved to a balanced point. The bottom row is especially important because students often diagonalize A and then stop. The null direction still needs to be interrogated for surviving affine information.

slides.title: Normal Form Ledger
slides.notes: This slide converts the classification table into a lab protocol. Emphasize that the names are conclusions, not inputs. The same symbolic equation can look unfamiliar until rank, signature, remaining linear terms, and level are recorded. The real field matters because signs cannot be erased there, while over the complex field the rank and affine residue carry more of the classification.

slides.title: Signs Become Shapes
slides.notes: This slide is deliberately visual but still algebraic. Ask the class to say which part of the equation is responsible for each shape feature. The goal is not to identify every surface from a thumbnail. It is to build a reflex: signs tell whether directions are confined or escaping, and rank deficiency tells whether an affine direction survives outside the quadratic part.

slides.title: Topology From Normal Form
slides.notes: Treat the slice diagram as a topology detector. The slices are not a proof by themselves, but they make the theorem believable and memorable. The important teaching point is that affine classification carries qualitative information. Once the normal form is known, we can predict compactness, components, ends, and singular points before plotting a dense surface.

slides.title: Polarity From Homogenization
slides.notes: This is where the affine chapter reconnects to projective quadrics without losing the affine viewpoint. Homogenization adds the coordinate at infinity and packages the equation into one symmetric matrix C. The pay-off is computational: the same multiplication CP gives tangent lines for points on the conic and polar lines for points away from it.

slides.title: Tangent Planes And Diameters
slides.notes: Keep the focus on reuse of matrix data. Students may think tangent planes, polar lines, and conjugate diameters are separate classical constructions. Here they are different readings of the same bilinear structure. The derivative gives tangent directions; homogenization gives polarity; centering turns the bilinear form into a rule for which chord families bisect each other.

slides.title: Euclidean Normal Forms
slides.notes: This slide separates affine and Euclidean classification cleanly. In affine geometry, all nondegenerate ellipsoids are equivalent after a suitable invertible change of coordinates. In Euclidean geometry, that is too coarse because rotations and translations cannot change the semi-axis lengths. The spectral theorem is therefore not just algebra; it is the bridge from type to measurement.

slides.title: Classify From Samples
slides.notes: This is the practical payoff slide. A dataset rarely arrives in principal-axis coordinates, so classification has to survive rotation, translation, and numerical noise. The residual ledger makes the computation auditable. Each small number corresponds to a claim made earlier in the lecture: the center equation, the diagonal form, the zero set condition, and the normalized axis equation.

slides.title: Pitfalls
slides.notes: Use the pitfalls as a short oral diagnostic. Each warning corresponds to a common premature conclusion: stopping after diagonalization, confusing the center with a point of the surface, forgetting the constant level, or moving between real and complex fields without noticing that signs have changed meaning. The metric caution prepares students for the Euclidean conic material that follows later.

slides.title: Exercise
slides.notes: Give students a minute to classify before showing any plot. The matrix has rank two and a null direction in z. The linear term in that null direction cannot be translated away, so the object has no center and should be an elliptic paraboloid. The exercise reinforces the main habit: diagnose algebraically first, then draw.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the lecture's promise. The chapter is not a bag of surface names; it is a workflow for extracting geometry from a quadratic equation. The reduction tells the affine story, homogenization recovers polarity, and Euclidean structure adds measured axes. The computational checks in the notebook are the discipline that keeps all three readings honest.
